Pathology of the Heart

Pathology Lab LE 2 · 04 · Dr. Florido Aban Atibagos

Lecture at a glance

A pathology lab built around five cases of the CVS. For each, the learner must examine and describe the gross alterations, describe the microscopic lesion by routine H & E, and correlate the clinical signs, symptoms and laboratory abnormalities with the tissue changes.

Case 1Acute Myocardial Infarction
→
Case 2Rheumatic Heart Disease
→

Case 4Infective Endocarditis
→

Must Know anchors AMI: know what is seen at each post-infarction time point, grossly and histologically.
RHD: Aschoff nodule is the typical lesion. Commissural fusion ("fish-mouth") is pathognomonic of chronic RHD.
IE: vegetations are large, bulky, friable, vs. small and warty in RHD.
Myocarditis: viral, mostly Coxsackieviruses A and B.
Myxoma: interatrial septum is the most common location. Stellate cells in myxoid stroma.

Learning objectives Slide 3

  • Demonstrate knowledge of the pathology of the CVS by:
    • Examining and describing the gross alterations of the lesion
    • Examining and describing the microscopic lesion by routine H & E stain preparation
  • Correlate clinical signs and symptoms with the expected pathologic changes by:
    • Explaining and interpreting signs and symptoms on the basis of tissue changes
    • Enumerating and explaining the laboratory abnormalities based on tissue changes
  • List down other possible conditions responsible for the signs and symptoms

Case 1: Acute Myocardial Infarction Slides 4–21, 52–55, 69–70

Case

  • A 71-year-old diabetic male admitted because of severe precordial pain, with sweating and diaphoresis.
  • Pain: crushing, persistent, with radiation to the left arm and back.
  • 48 hours after admission, died of arrhythmia and congestive heart failure.

Gross

Area of infarction Must Know Slides 5, 16

  • Appears pale and yellow tan
  • Usually surrounded by areas of hyperemia
  • Remaining viable myocardium appears reddish-brown

Sectioning and cut surface Slide 6

  • Breadloaf Technique: sectioning the heart by slicing the ventricles from the fibrous annulus until the apex of the heart.
  • Areas of infarction appear to be pale or white (black pointed arrow).
    • Also seen: the Interventricular Septum and Papillary Muscles.
  • Sometimes there could be a superimposed thrombus or mural thrombus (thrombus within the muscular wall).

Histology: post-infarction time course

Lecture stages Must Know Slides 7–12, 17–18

Time post-infarctionHistologic features
First 24 hours
  • Contraction bands
  • Eosinophilia of myocardial fibers
  • Loss of nuclei and striations in myocardial fibers
  • Presence of inflammatory cells between the myocardium (early infiltration)
  • Extensive hemorrhage
3rd to 4th day
  • Neutrophils are either:
    • Replaced by mononuclear infiltrates (extensive acute inflammatory cell infiltrate)
    • Undergoing apoptosis, karyorrhexis, and karyolysis
  • Myocardial fibers undergoing necrosis: outlines are not well-defined
  • Few striations and cell nuclei no longer visible
  • Serum troponin increase
1st to 2nd week
  • Normal myocardium remain
  • Infarcted myocardium slowly replaced by:
    • Mononuclear infiltrates
    • Neovascularization
    • Scanty collagen
  • Necrotic myocardium cleared by macrophages, early collagen deposition (beginning stage of scar formation)
3rd to 4th week
  • Infarcted area appears pale and has been slowly replaced by collagen
  • Cleansed by macrophage (less mononuclear infiltrates) → replaced by fibrous tissue (collagen)
  • Presence of neovascularization
Recall Heart is a permanent tissue.
Once damaged, myocardium cannot regenerate and is instead replaced by a fibrous scar tissue.
Clinical cue Clinically, AMI is marked by changes in ECG (STEMI and NSTEMI) and a rise in Troponin I & T and CK-MB.

Histology figures by stage

Robbins time course (Lab Exercise rationales) Must Know Slides 53, 55, 70

TimeGrossHisto
12–24 hoursDark mottlingOngoing coagulation necrosis.
Pyknosis of nuclei.
Myocyte hypereosinophilia.
Marginal contraction band necrosis.
Beginning of neutrophilic infiltrate.
3–7 daysHyperemic border.
Central yellow-tan softening.		Beginning disintegration of dead myofibers with dying neutrophils.
Early phagocytosis of dead cells by macrophages at infarct border.
10–14 daysRed-gray depressed infarct bordersWell-established granulation tissue with new blood vessels and collagen deposition

Exam trap (from lab exercises and formative quiz) First 24 hours, histo: contraction bands. Not neutrophil apoptosis (3–7 days), not start of collagen deposition (2–8 weeks), not neovascularization (10–14 days).
First 24 hours, gross: dark mottling. Central yellow-tan softening is 3–7 days. Red-gray borders are 10–14 days.
On the third day, gross: hyperemic borders (3rd to 7th day). Grayish white scar is 2 to 8 weeks. Reddish-gray border is 10th to 14th day.

Cell necrosis and infarct margins (virtual slides)

Cell necrosis is shown by Slides 13, 18

  • Increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia
    • Eosin: an acidic dye. Staining is increased following exposure of basic amino acids on denatured proteins.
  • Loss of nuclei

Margins of the infarct Slides 14–15, 19

  • Around the margins of infarct: some ingress of acute inflammatory cells into the dead tissue.
  • Polymorphs: band of blue-stained cells with nuclear debris released from dead fibers.
    • Drawn by chemotactic effects of tissue breakdown products (denatured proteins and released enzymes).
  • Dead fibers are interspersed with a small number of polymorphs. In the center the fibers have disappeared → replaced by areas of hemorrhage.
  • Bluish areas could be pooled DNA or precipitated calcium salts.

Study guide: risk factors and diagnostics

Factors associated with MI: Nonmodifiable factors Slide 20

Age

  • MI frequency rises progressively with increasing age
  • MI incidence increases fivefold between ages 40 and 60
    • Nearly 10% of myocardial infarcts occur in people younger than 40
    • 45% occur in people younger than 65

Genetic & Behavioral Dispositions to Atherosclerosis

Sex

  • Middle-aged male gender increases the risk of MI
  • Women are generally protected against MI during reproductive years
    • However, postmenopausal decline in estrogen → accelerated coronary artery disease
  • Ischemic heart disease: most common cause of death in older women

4 diagnostic tests in AMI Must Know Slide 21

TestClinical usefulness
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Helps detect arrhythmias and allows for prompt defibrillation
Biomarkers (cardiac-specific troponins T and I)Indicators of necrotic myocytes, as necrotic myocytes leak these into the bloodstream.
Helps differentiate NSTEMI (elevated cardiac biomarkers) from Unstable Angina (normal).
Cardiac Imaging (coronary angiography, PET, echocardiography)Helps rule out coronary artery disease when MI is suspected.
Defines the degree of myocardial perfusion abnormality.
  • Coronary angiography: gold standard for identifying the location and severity of coronary artery stenosis or thrombosis
  • Echocardiography: measure of ejection fraction (EF) and can identify regional wall motion abnormalities, which are hallmarks of myocardial damage
Complete Blood CountUsed to prognosticate.
High neutrophil count: poor prognosis.

Case 2: Rheumatic Heart Disease Slides 22–33, 56–61, 71–72

Case

  • A 12 year-old girl with a 6-week history of painful, swollen joints and recent onset dyspnea.
  • PE: temperature of 38C, cervical lymphadenopathy, pansystolic and diastolic murmurs.
  • Lab: positive for serum antibodies to streptolysin O.
  • Died of progressive heart failure. On autopsy, the heart weighed 380 grams.

Definition and background Must Know Slide 23

  • Rheumatic Heart Disease is a consequence of repeated bouts of rheumatic fever.
  • Rheumatic fever is caused by pharyngitis secondary to Group A Beta-hemolytic Streptococcus.
  • Has autoimmune background secondary to a cross reacting antibody against Streptococcal cell wall
    • which cannot distinguish between the Streptococcal cell wall and antigens present in the cardiac valves, myocardium and endocardium
    • leading to destruction of cardiac valves and myocardium

Etiopathogenesis Must Know Slide 31

1. Initial Streptococcal InfectionAfter group A streptococcus pharyngitis, host produces anti-strep antibodies against streptococcal antigens such as M protein.
→
2. Cross ReactivityM protein shares structural similarity with host proteins including cardiac myosin. Immune system mistakenly attacks host tissues.
→
3. Autoimmune ReactionCross-reactive antibodies (Type II Hypersensitivity) and CD4+ T lymphocytes recognize native host proteins in the heart (and joints) as "foreign".
→
4. Tissue DamageSystemic inflammatory response causes vegetations in the mitral valve, Aschoff nodules in myocardium and pericardium, and "bread and butter" fibrinous pericarditis.

Gross

Mitral valve and pericardium Slides 24–26

  • Mitral valve with small, warty vegetations.
  • "Fish mouth appearance" of the mitral valve (mitral stenosis from RHD).
  • Fibrinous Pericarditis
    • Acute stage of Rheumatic Heart Disease
    • "Bread and butter" pericarditis

Mitral valve changes in chronic RHD Must Know Slide 59

ChangeLecture rationale
Commissural fusion ✔The pathognomonic lesion of chronic RHD, producing the classic "fish-mouth appearance" along areas of closure of mitral valve
Cuspal fusionCusps become thickened and fibrotic, but true fusion of the cusps is not the hallmark lesion
Chordae tendineaeChordae tendineae are shortened and thickened
Valve leafletsBecome rigid, fibrotic, and thickened, not softened

Histology

Aschoff Nodule Must Know Slides 27, 57, 72

  • Typical lesion in Rheumatic Heart Disease
  • A localized area of inflammation and necrosis
  • Composed of inflammatory cells such as lymphocytes (T lymphocytes), plasma cells, macrophages, and Anitschkow myocytes (transformed macrophages), seen in HPO
ComponentIn the Aschoff nodule?
T cellsYes. Primarily involved in the inflammatory response, mostly CD4+
B cellsNo (the EXCEPT answer). While plasma cells are seen, B cells themselves are not a characteristic component
MacrophagesYes. Specifically Anitschkow cells (activated macrophages)
Plasma cellsYes. Part of chronic inflammation

Anitschkow cells Must Know Slides 28–30, 61

  • Found in Aschoff Nodules (HPO)
  • Transformed monocytes or macrophages
    • They are NOT giant cells in Aschoff nodules
  • In cut or cross-section: "owl eye nuclei" appearance
  • Chromatin described as fine and wavy, assuming a caterpillar appearance, known as "caterpillar cells"
  • Abundant cytoplasm and central, ovoid nuclei with condensed chromatin
From Robbins and Cotran The myocardium exhibits a circumscribed nodule of mixed mononuclear inflammatory cells with associated necrosis.
Within the inflammation, large activated macrophages show prominent nuclei and chromatin condensed into long, wavy ribbons (caterpillar cells).
Do not confuse Anitschkow cells: classic modified macrophages in Aschoff nodules of RHD, "caterpillar-like".
Epithelioid cells: activated macrophages with elongated nuclei in granulomatous inflammation such as tuberculosis, not specific for rheumatic fever.
Owl cells: Reed–Sternberg cells of Hodgkin lymphoma, large nuclei with prominent nucleoli resembling "owl's eyes".

Diagnosis

Jones criteria for Rheumatic Fever Must Know Slide 32

Diagnosis requires: evidence of a preceding group A streptococcal infection, plus either:

  • 2 major criteria, or
  • 1 major criterion + 2 minor criteria
Major criteriaMinor criteria
  • Pancarditis ✔
  • Polyarthritis ✔
  • Sydenham's chorea
  • Erythema marginatum
  • Subcutaneous nodules
  • Fever ✔
  • Arthralgia ✔
  • Elevated ESR/CRP
  • Prolonged PR interval (ECG)
Clinical features satisfied in this patient (✔) Preceding streptococcal infection, (+) ASO.
Pancarditis (pansystolic and diastolic murmurs).
Painful, swollen joints.
Fever.

Expected abnormal laboratory tests Slide 33

Laboratory testExpected resultReason for abnormality
Streptococcal Antibodies
  • Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer
  • Anti-DNase B
ElevatedProduced in response to a Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) infection
Acute Phase Reactants
  • Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)
  • C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
ElevatedNonspecific markers of inflammation increased due to the immune response to streptococcal antigens
Exam trap (lab exercise) Cardiac lesion seen in RHD: Aschoff nodule.
Bulky friable vegetations are seen in Infective Endocarditis, not RHD.

Case 3: Myocarditis Slides 34–36, 64–65, 77–78

Case

  • A 45-year-old female admitted for low grade fever, exertional dyspnea, mild to moderate chest pain, with palpitations and fatigue.
  • Claimed to have flu-like symptoms 2 weeks ago.

Definition and etiology Must Know Slides 34, 65

  • Myocarditis is the inflammation of the heart muscle caused by a broad range of infections or immune reactions.
  • The most common cause of myocarditis is a viral infection:
    • Coxsackieviruses A and B (most common)
    • Enteroviruses
    • Cytomegalovirus
    • HIV
    • Influenza virus
  • Lab exercise rationale: less common: CMV, HIV, Influenza, COVID.
Exam trap Etiology of myocarditis: Viruses. Not "all of the above" (gram positive bacteria, acid fast bacilli).

Histology Must Know Slides 35–36

  • Presence of inflammatory cells, mostly composed of mononuclear cells such as lymphocytes and macrophages.
  • Presence of interstitial inflammatory cells which are predominantly lymphocytes.

Gross: acute vs. advanced Slide 78

StageGross morphology
AcuteHeart may appear normal or dilated.
"Dilated with focal hypertrophy" may be seen in acute, not advanced, myocarditis.
AdvancedMyocardium is typically flabby and often mottled with pale and hemorrhagic areas.
Mural thrombi may be present.

Case 4: Infective Endocarditis Slides 37–47, 62–63, 73–74

Case

  • A 30-year old female admitted for exertional dyspnea, fever, and chills of 2 weeks duration.
  • Diagnosed with Rheumatic Heart Disease with Mitral Stenosis and Aortic Insufficiency at 14 years of age.
  • On admission: temperature 39°C, RR 30/min, HR 120/min.
  • Chest auscultation: bi-basal rales with loud blowing murmur heard best at Erb's point.
  • Died of intractable heart failure.

How would someone with RHD develop IE? Must Know Slide 38

  • Damaged, scarred valves act as a nidus for bacterial colonization during transient bacteremia.
  • Bacteria could erode the ventricular septum → acquired septal defect.
  • Streptococcus viridans remains the most common causative organism.
    • Other pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus and HACEK organisms.
  • Consequences: valve destruction, systemic embolization, and life-threatening complications.
HACEK Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella

Definition and causes Must Know Slide 39

  • Colonization of heart valves and mural endocardium by microbiological agents, forming bulky vegetations.
    • Vegetations contain thrombotic material, inflammatory cells, and microbiologic organisms.

Causes:

  • Bacteria: Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Pneumococci, etc.
  • Fungi: Aspergillosis, Candida, Mucormycosis, etc.
  • Rickettsia
  • Chlamydia

Acute vs. Subacute IE Must Know Slide 40

FeatureAcute Infective EndocarditisSubacute Infective Endocarditis
OrganismCaused by highly virulent organismsCaused by low virulent organisms (Enterococci, Streptococcus viridans)
ValveArises in a normal valveOccurs in previously diseased valves (congenital valve anomaly, RHD, MV prolapse, etc.)
LesionNecrotizing, ulcerative, and destructive lesions.
Bulky, friable vegetations.		—
ClinicalMore severe clinical signs and symptoms (higher morbidity)Insidious clinical onset

Etiologic agents (lab exercise) Must Know Slide 63

OrganismLecture rationale
Staphylococcus aureus ✔
(usual agent with normal valves)		Can infect either healthy or deformed valves.
Causes Acute bacterial endocarditis within days.
Streptococcus viridansMost common overall cause in previously damaged valves.
Slow developing subacute bacterial endocarditis.
Streptococcus pyogenesGroup A strep, typically causing pharyngitis and rheumatic fever
Haemophilus sp.HACEK organism associated with endocarditis with (-) blood cultures

Clinical features Slide 41

Presents with:

  • Fever
  • Weight loss
  • Fatigue, anorexia, changing murmurs

Laboratory diagnosis:

  • Leukocytosis
  • Positive blood culture
ComplicationsFindings
Cardiac
  • CHF
  • Valve insufficiency/stenosis
  • Myocardial ring
  • Abscess
  • Suppurative pericarditis
  • Valvular rupture
Embolic
  • Roth spots
  • Subungual and cerebrovascular hemorrhages
Renal
  • Embolic infarcts
  • Focal/diffuse glomerulonephritis
  • Abscesses

Gross

Vegetations Must Know Slides 42–44, 74

  • Characteristics: large, soft, friable, easily detached vegetations consisting of fibrin and intermeshed inflammatory cells and bacteria.
  • Usually seen in the cusps of the valve, sometimes extending to the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
Key differentiator: comparison with RHD In RHD, the vegetations are small and warty, located along the lines of closure of the valves.
In Infective Endocarditis, vegetations are large, bulky, and friable, in the valvular cusps with extensions to the chordae tendineae.

Histology

Microscopic features Slides 45–47

  • Lesions are composed of inflammatory cells, bacterial colonies, and some fibrin.
  • In HPO, the basophilic structures are made up of bacterial colonies, inflammatory cells (mostly polymorphonuclear cells), and some fibrin.
  • Bacterial colonies appear as purplish clumps.

Case 5: Cardiac Myxoma Slides 48–50, 66–67, 75–76

Case

  • A 23 year old female complains of difficulty of breathing when lying flat on bed.
  • Occasional chest pains and tachycardia.

Gross Must Know Slides 48, 67

  • Gelatinous mass surrounded by hemorrhages
  • Can be seen attached to atrial septum or mitral valve leaflet
    • Most common location: interatrial septum. Most of the time, the myxoma is attached to the atrial septum.
    • Sometimes it could also attach to the leaflet of the mitral valve.

Histology Must Know Slides 49–50, 76

  • Myxomas are composed of stellate or star-shaped (typically hyperchromatic nuclei) cells in a myxoid background.
  • Classic histologic hallmark: scattered stellate or globular myxoma cells embedded in an abundant loose myxoid matrix, often with areas of hemorrhage and inflammation.
Option (formative quiz)Lecture rationale
Stellate shaped cells in a myxoid stroma ✔The classic histologic hallmark of cardiac myxomas
Multinucleated cells in a myxoid backgroundNot typical. Multinucleated giant cells are not a hallmark of myxomas.
Few plump modified macrophages in a myxoid backgroundMacrophages may occasionally be present but are not the defining feature
Spindle shaped cells in a myxoid stromaCan be seen, but not the classic or most distinctive finding

Core definitions

  • RHD: consequence of repeated bouts of rheumatic fever, caused by pharyngitis from Group A Beta-hemolytic Streptococcus.
  • Myocarditis: inflammation of the heart muscle caused by a broad range of infections or immune reactions.
  • Infective Endocarditis: colonization of heart valves and mural endocardium by microbiological agents, forming bulky vegetations.
  • Aschoff nodule: typical lesion in RHD. A localized area of inflammation and necrosis.
  • Anitschkow cells: transformed monocytes or macrophages in Aschoff nodules. Not giant cells.
  • Breadloaf technique: slicing the ventricles from the fibrous annulus until the apex.

AMI time course

TimeGrossHisto
12–24 hDark mottlingContraction bands, hypereosinophilia, loss of nuclei and striations, hemorrhage, early neutrophils
3–7 daysHyperemic border, central yellow-tan softeningDying neutrophils (apoptosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis), early macrophage phagocytosis
10–14 days (1st–2nd wk)Red-gray depressed bordersGranulation tissue: new vessels, mononuclear cells, scanty collagen
2–8 weeks (3rd–4th wk)Gray-white scarCollagen ↑, cellularity ↓
Must Know Heart is a permanent tissue: myocardium cannot regenerate → replaced by fibrous scar.
Cell necrosis = increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia + loss of nuclei.
Eosin is an acidic dye binding basic amino acids exposed on denatured proteins.

AMI gross, risk and diagnostics

Gross

  • Infarct: pale and yellow tan
  • Surrounded by hyperemia
  • Viable myocardium: reddish-brown
  • Possible mural thrombus

Diagnostic tests

  • ECG: arrhythmias, prompt defibrillation
  • Troponins T and I: necrotic myocytes
    • NSTEMI ↑ vs. Unstable Angina normal
  • Coronary angiography: gold standard for location and severity of stenosis/thrombosis
  • Echo: EF, regional wall motion abnormalities
  • CBC: high neutrophils = poor prognosis
Important valuesAnchor
MI incidenceFivefold ↑ between ages 40 and 60
MI < 40 years oldNearly 10%
MI < 65 years old45%
WomenProtected in reproductive years. Postmenopausal estrogen decline → accelerated CAD. IHD = most common cause of death in older women.
Jones criteriaPreceding GAS infection + 2 major or 1 major + 2 minor

RHD essentials

1GAS pharyngitis → anti-strep antibodies vs. M protein
→
2Cross reactivity: M protein resembles cardiac myosin
→
3Type II hypersensitivity + CD4+ T cells
→
4Mitral vegetations, Aschoff nodules, bread and butter pericarditis

Jones criteria

Major:

  • Pancarditis
  • Polyarthritis
  • Sydenham's chorea
  • Erythema marginatum
  • Subcutaneous nodules

Minor:

  • Fever
  • Arthralgia
  • Elevated ESR/CRP
  • Prolonged PR interval

Morphology

  • Small, warty mitral vegetations
  • Commissural fusion = pathognomonic of chronic RHD → fish-mouth
  • Chordae: shortened and thickened
  • Leaflets: rigid, fibrotic, not softened
  • Fibrinous pericarditis = acute stage ("bread and butter")
  • Aschoff: T cells (CD4+), plasma cells, Anitschkow cells. Not B cells.
  • Labs: ASO, anti-DNase B, ESR, CRP elevated

IE complications

  • Cardiac: CHF, valve insufficiency/stenosis, myocardial ring, abscess, suppurative pericarditis, valvular rupture
  • Embolic: Roth spots, subungual and cerebrovascular hemorrhages
  • Renal: embolic infarcts, focal/diffuse glomerulonephritis, abscesses

Common exam traps Owl cells = Reed–Sternberg (Hodgkin), not Anitschkow cells.
Epithelioid cells = granulomatous inflammation (TB), not RHD.
B cells are not a characteristic Aschoff nodule component.
S. pyogenes causes rheumatic fever, not the usual IE agent.
Bulky friable vegetations = IE. Small warty = RHD.
Third day gross MI = hyperemic borders, not scar.
